title: When Talwiinder Jumped on Stage in Toronto, the Internet Lost Its Mind
excerpt: An Indian singer's surprise appearance at a Pakistani artist's concert ignited a firestorm — and a debate diaspora communities know all too well
body:
On May 9, Punjabi singer Talwiinder made an unannounced appearance at Pakistani artist Hasan Raheem's concert in Toronto, part of Raheem's "Dil Kay Parday" North American tour. The two performed their 2023 collaboration "Wishes" before a roaring crowd, then danced together to "Nach Punjaban." Talwiinder posted photos and video clips to Instagram. Within hours, the comments section had become a battlefield.

**The backlash was swift and fierce.** "Shame on you," read the most-shared refrain, repeated thousands of times across X (formerly Twitter), Instagram, and YouTube. Critics accused Talwiinder of insensitivity, pointing to heightened India-Pakistan tensions following the Pahalgam attack earlier this year. Several users dug up old social media posts in which Raheem had allegedly mocked Indian artists and ridiculed Operation Sindoor, India's retaliatory military action. The cross-border optics, critics argued, were indefensible.

**But the defence was just as vocal.** Supporters framed the collaboration as precisely the kind of cultural bridge-building South Asia needs. "Music doesn't carry a passport," one widely shared post argued. Others noted that Talwiinder and Raheem had been friends and collaborators for years — their partnership predating the current political crisis by a wide margin. Several Indian-Canadian fans who attended the Toronto show described the atmosphere as electric, with audiences of both nationalities singing along in unison.

**For diaspora audiences, the tension is achingly familiar.** In cities like Toronto, London, and Dubai — where Indian and Pakistani communities live side by side, share grocery stores and cricket leagues — the line between solidarity and betrayal is policed with unusual ferocity on social media, even when it barely registers in person. The Talwiinder episode is the latest in a pattern: the Indian student in London who was doxxed for attending a Pakistani Independence Day event; the restaurateur in New Jersey who faced boycott calls for hosting a joint Diwali-Eid dinner.

**Talwiinder, for his part, has said nothing.** His Instagram post from the concert remains up, gathering equal measures of adoration and abuse. Raheem, too, has stayed quiet, though he shared clips of the performance to his own following. Neither artist appears inclined to apologise or explain.

**The episode raises questions that go beyond two singers and one concert.** South Asian music has been quietly building a cross-border ecosystem for years. Coke Studio Pakistan features Indian guests. Spotify playlists blend Bollywood and Pakistani indie without friction. Diaspora festivals in North America routinely book artists from both countries on the same bill. The audience for this music — young, global, raised on streaming rather than state television — generally does not sort its playlists by nationality.

**Yet the internet does.** And in the aftermath of Pahalgam, the political temperature makes every cultural gesture a potential flashpoint. For NRI and Pakistani-diaspora listeners in Toronto, the show was a Friday night out. For social media's self-appointed border patrol, it was treason.

**What comes next will be telling.** If Talwiinder addresses the controversy, he risks satisfying neither side. If he stays silent, the news cycle will likely move on within days. But the underlying tension — between art that crosses borders and politics that fortifies them — is not going anywhere, least of all in the diaspora cities where both communities have made their lives.
